title: Approximate complex amplitude encoding algorithm and its application to data classification problems
abstract_summary: The paper introduces ACAE (approximate complex amplitude encoding), an extension of approximate amplitude encoding to load complex-valued classical data into shallow parametrized quantum circuits by using fidelity as the cost function and classical shadows for efficient fidelity estimation. The authors apply ACAE to implement a compact Hadamard classifier for binary classification, demonstrate proof-of-concept results on the Iris dataset and a credit card fraud detection task, and discuss scaling and practical challenges such as fidelity estimation and barren plateaus.
methodology_description: The authors develop an Approximate Complex Amplitude Encoding (ACAE) algorithm that extends prior Approximate Amplitude Encoding to complex-valued classical vectors. ACAE trains a shallow parametrized quantum circuit (PQC) U(θ) to prepare a model state |ψ(θ)⟩ whose amplitudes approximate a given complex target vector up to a global phase. The fidelity f(θ)=|⟨Data|ψ(θ)⟩|^2 is used as the cost function (replacing MMD which cannot distinguish complex phases). Fidelity (and its gradients via parameter-shift) is estimated efficiently using the classical-shadow protocol with random Clifford measurements; the inverse shadow channel M^{-1}(·) = (2^n + 1)· − I is applied to classical snapshots to produce unbiased fidelity estimates. The PQC uses a hardware-efficient ansatz (layers of single-qubit Rx,Ry,Rz rotations and CNOTs) and is trained by gradient-based optimization (parameter-shift rule combined with the Adam optimizer). ACAE is combined with the Compact Hadamard Classifier (CHC): training data pairs (real vectors for two classes) are embedded into real and imaginary parts of amplitudes of a joint state via ACAE; a second PQC U'(θ') encodes test vectors; a Hadamard on an ancilla and measurement of ⟨σ_z⟩ on that ancilla yields a kernel-like decision score (sign of ⟨σ_z⟩). Numerical demonstrations include Iris classification and a credit-card fraud detection proof-of-concept, where small subsets of the public datasets are amplitude-encoded and classification is performed using the ACAE+CHC pipeline.
experimental_setup: Numerical simulations / classical experiments. Fidelity estimates were obtained via classical-shadow sampling using random Clifford unitaries; stabilizer-based simulation (Gottesman-Knill) was used to compute required amplitudes/overlaps for Clifford elements. No specific quantum hardware backend is specified; the authors acknowledge use of IBM Quantum services but do not report a particular QPU or simulator name for the presented numerical experiments.
dataset_used: Iris dataset (standard 3-class dataset; authors used pairwise binary classification subsets) and the Kaggle credit card fraud detection dataset (European cardholders, Sep 2013) containing 284,807 transactions with 492 fraudulent transactions. For demonstrations, small subsets were used.

pipeline_steps: Prepare initial ancilla/register state |ψ0⟩ with Hadamard, Rz(ϕ) and weighting Uw(b) to form a superposition over training indices and ancilla branches (training vs test).

Train a multi-qubit PQC U(θ) (hardware-efficient ansatz) to map basis data registers to amplitude-encoded training data in the data register conditioned on ancilla/index states, by maximizing fidelity f(θ) between the PQC output state and the target amplitude-encoded state. Fidelity is estimated by constructing classical shadows from repeated random Clifford measurements on the model state and applying M^{-1} to the measurement snapshots.
Compute gradients via parameter-shift rule: evaluate fidelity at θ±π/2 for each parameter and form finite differences; use these estimates in Adam optimizer to update θ.
For each test vector, train a smaller PQC U'(θ') (Ry-only layers + CNOTs when test vector is real) to encode the test vector into the data register in the ancilla=|1⟩ branch.
Apply Hadamard to the ancilla qubit and measure ⟨σ_z⟩ on ancilla. The classifier outputs sign(⟨σ_z⟩) as predicted label.
Report fidelity of state preparation and classification outcomes (⟨σ_z⟩ values and resulting labels).

key_findings: [supported] The paper introduces ACAE (approximate complex amplitude encoding), an extension of AAE that can load complex-valued classical vectors into amplitudes of shallow parametrized quantum circuits by optimizing fidelity between model and target states.

[supported] ACAE uses the fidelity as the cost function (instead of MMD used in AAE) and employs the classical shadow protocol with random Clifford measurements to estimate fidelity and its gradients efficiently for the training process.

[supported] In small-scale numerical simulations, ACAE-trained PQCs achieved high fidelities: example training fidelity reached ~0.994 for the Iris training PQC and >0.999 for per-test-data PQCs in their demonstrations.

[supported] The authors integrated ACAE with the compact Hadamard classifier (CHC) to realize a complex-valued-kernel binary classifier using polynomial-depth PQCs in place of exponential-depth exact amplitude encoders and uniformly-controlled gates; they demonstrated correct classifications in small proof-of-principle tests (Iris subsets and a small subset of credit-card fraud data).

[supported] Empirical demonstrations: Iris (setosa vs versicolor) classification: 8/8 correct for chosen test instances; Iris (versicolor vs virginica) mixed results with some misclassifications attributed to dataset overlap and encoding errors; credit-card fraud detection on a selected small subset: 8/8 correct for chosen test instances, and 42/48 correct in an additional random sample of 48 instances.

[supported] Practical parameters used in demonstrations: 5 qubits (n+m+1) to encode 4-dimensional features across 8 data items, Nshot = 1000 classical snapshots per fidelity estimate, and standard optimizers (Adam) with specified learning-rate schedules.

[supported] The paper identifies key limitations: (a) fidelity is a global cost and vulnerable to barren-plateau (gradient vanishing) effects for larger systems, and (b) sampling classical shadows with random Clifford unitaries can require substantial entangling-gate depth in practice.

[speculative] The authors claim potential to implement CHC with significantly fewer gates than exact amplitude encoding and thereby enable more compact quantum classifiers; while this is theoretically plausible and supported at small scale, demonstration of advantage at practically relevant sizes is not provided.

[speculative] The paper suggests ACAE could be applied to larger practical tasks in finance (e.g., fraud detection on real-world large datasets) and to state preparation in quantum chemistry, but scalability and training obstacles (depth increase, barren plateaus) are acknowledged and remain open.

[speculative] The authors discuss mitigation strategies for scaling issues (localized fidelity measurements, special ansatz, parameter initialization/embedding) as future directions; these are recommendations rather than demonstrated solutions in this work.
results_summary: The paper proposes ACAE, a variational method to approximate complex-valued amplitude encoding by maximizing fidelity between a target complex-amplitude state and a shallow PQC-generated model state. Fidelity estimation and gradients are obtained using the classical-shadow protocol with random Clifford measurements. ACAE is combined with the compact Hadamard classifier to build a complex-kernel binary classifier without exponential-depth state-preparation circuits. Small-scale numerical demonstrations (Iris subsets and a small credit-card fraud subset) show high fidelity state preparation (e.g., ~0.994) and correct classifications in the chosen test instances. The authors also analyze scalability concerns (increasing circuit depth with qubit number, barren-plateau risk, and Clifford sampling cost) and outline potential mitigation strategies as future work.
performance_claims: Training fidelity reached approximately 0.994 for the Iris training PQC (5-qubit, 12-layer ansatz) after 400 optimization iterations (Nshot = 1000).
Per-test-data PQC fidelities exceeded 0.999 in the Iris demonstrations (2-qubit, 2-layer Ry-only ansatz), trained with 100 iterations and Nshot = 1000.
Iris classification: setosa vs versicolor: 8/8 tested instances correctly classified in their demonstration.
Iris classification: versicolor vs virginica: 5/8 tested instances correctly classified when using ACAE-encoded data; when using exact (ideal) encoding, all 8/8 tested instances were correct.
Credit-card fraud detection (selected small subset): 8/8 tested instances correctly classified in the main run; additional random sample: 42/48 correctly classified.
For demonstrations the circuit used 5 qubits (n+m+1 = 5) to encode 4 feature dimensions across 8 data examples (N = 4, M = 8).
Classical-shadow sampling used Nshot = 1000 snapshots per fidelity estimate in demonstrations.

Observed that required PQC depth to reach target fidelities (0.90, 0.95, 0.99) increases superlinearly with number of qubits (examined up to 9 qubits / 1024-classical-data setting); for 5 qubits, reducing fidelity to ~0.7 still yielded >80% classification accuracy in that specific setting.
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors argue that ACAE enables approximate complex amplitude encoding and thus allows implementing the compact Hadamard classifier using shallow (polynomial-depth) PQCs instead of exponential-depth exact state preparation, which could reduce resource requirements for certain quantum classifiers. However, this paper provides small-scale demonstrations only and does not demonstrate a practical or asymptotic quantum computational advantage; scalability and training challenges (depth growth, barren plateaus, Clifford sampling cost) remain open.
limitations: Scalability: required variational circuit depth increases superlinearly with number of qubits; ACAE may not be applicable to large-scale problems (authors' simulation shows increasing depth from 5 to 9 qubits) (explicit).
Global-cost optimization: using fidelity as a cost yields a global cost function that is prone to barren plateaus / gradient vanishing as system size grows (explicit).

Classical-shadow measurement overhead: fidelity estimation via random Clifford measurements requires O(n^2 / log2(n)) entangling gates to sample n-qubit Cliffords, which is a practical drawback (explicit).
Classical postprocessing cost: evaluating terms like ⟨b_i| U_i |k⟩ and the sums in Eq. (12) involve O(2^n) classical computations (explicit), so classical resources grow exponentially with data size.
Per-test online encoding: the test-data encoder U'(θ') is trained per test datum (online), which adds runtime and may limit throughput in prediction settings (explicit).

Limited empirical validation: demonstrations are on small-scale problems (Iris and small subsets of a credit-card dataset), so generalization to realistic, large financial datasets is unproven ([inferred]).

[inferred] Potential loss of end-to-end quantum advantage: because fidelity evaluation and some computations are done classically and scale exponentially, the net quantum/classical resource tradeoff may negate advantages for large datasets.
[inferred] Binary-classifier focus: the CHC formulation and demonstrations are for binary classification; extension to multiclass problems is not shown.

[inferred] Sensitivity of classification performance to imperfect fidelity: lower fidelity can still give acceptable accuracy for some problems, but the relationship between fidelity and classifier performance is problem-dependent and not fully characterized.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — ACAE (Approximate Complex Amplitude Encoding) enables loading complex-valued classical vectors into shallow parameterized quantum circuits, targeting NISQ-era implementability.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The pipeline combines a variational PQC for state preparation with classical-shadow tomography for fidelity estimation and classical optimizers (Adam + parameter-shift), i.e., a hybrid quantum-classical workflow.

#idea:hybrid-approach — ACAE is integrated with the Compact Hadamard Classifier (CHC) to form an end-to-end quantum classifier used for binary classification tasks (Iris subsets, credit-card fraud demo).

#limitation:simulation-only — All demonstrations are numerical/stabilizer-based simulations (Gottesman-Knill + classical-shadow sampling); no reported experiments on real QPUs for the presented results.
#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Results are shown on heavily subsampled datasets (few training/test points) and lack comparison to classical baselines or statistical significance testing.

#limitation:data-encoding — The paper highlights the cost and fidelity impact of approximate amplitude encoding and shows that approximation errors can directly degrade classification performance (examples where exact encoding corrected misclassifications).
#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstrations use very small circuits (n+m+1 = 5 qubits); authors explicitly discuss scaling challenges when moving to larger datasets/features.
#limitation:noise — The work discusses practical challenges such as barren plateaus and fidelity estimation overheads that would be exacerbated by QPU noise, though no noise experiments are reported.
